title: Detection of Spearphishing Attachment
summary: This detection strategy covers phishing for information that carries a file, where the attacker wants the target to open a document, archive or shortcut rather than simply click a link. The file is used to collect credentials, to start a conversation that reveals internal detail or to test whether the address is live. The telemetry that makes it visible is mail gateway records with attachment name, type and hash, mail client cache or download folder file creation events, sandbox verdicts and user reports. It fails in practice because archive files and password protected documents often pass content inspection, and a first contact message can look entirely ordinary.

beginner.definition: Phishing means a fake message that tries to make you act. A spearphishing attachment is a file that is sent with that message. The file may ask for a password or collect your details. This detection looks for suspicious files that arrive by mail and are then opened.
beginner.whyItMatters: Text only messages are easy to filter, so attackers now send files instead. A file gives the attacker more ways to hide the real purpose. It can carry a form that asks for a password, or a script that collects details quietly. The first message of a campaign often looks harmless. The attacker is only testing the address and the interest of the target. If you catch that first file, you can warn the user and block the sender before the real payload arrives.
howItWorks: Your mail gateway records the file name, file type, size and hash of every attachment.
It also records the sender, the authentication results and the delivery decision.
The detection flags file types that users rarely need, such as disk images and shortcut files.
File creation events from the mail client cache folder show that a user opened the file.
A sandbox report adds a verdict when the file was detonated in a safe environment.
An attachment that reaches a user and is then opened raises an alert with the message and the file.
beginner.example: Think of a parcel delivered to an office reception. Most parcels are expected and the label matches an order. Reception still checks the shape and the weight. A padded envelope claims to be from a supplier. It has no order number and a hand written label, so it deserves a second look. Your mail gateway is reception and the sandbox is the X ray machine. The detection is the rule that says unusual parcels must be checked before delivery. The file creation event is the record that somebody opened it.
takeaways: Attackers send files because plain text is easy to filter.
The first file in a campaign is often only a test of the address.
Join the mail record with the local file creation event for proof of open.

objectives: Define spearphishing attachment and describe the goal of the attacker.
List the mail gateway fields that describe an attachment.
Correlate a delivered message with a file created from the mail cache.
Explain how a sandbox verdict supports or weakens a decision.
Describe the user warning and containment steps for a delivered file.
dataSources: Secure email gateway message records with attachment file name, extension, size and hash value
Mail platform message trace and threat alerts showing delivery, quarantine or user report actions
Endpoint file creation events for the mail client cache and download folders, with the writing process
Sandbox detonation reports for attachments, including behaviour summary and network callbacks
User reported phishing mailbox submissions and the analyst verdict recorded for each one
logic: The pattern is an inbound message with an attachment type that has no business reason, delivered to a user and then written to disk by the mail client or browser, especially when the file is an archive, disk image or shortcut. The fields that must be correlated are the sender and its authentication results, the attachment name, extension and hash, the delivery action taken by the gateway, the process that created the file on the endpoint and any sandbox verdict for the same hash. Benign cases include scanned invoices as disk images from partners, password protected payroll files and personal documents sent by colleagues. The malicious case pairs a first contact sender with an attachment the recipient was not expecting and a file creation event seconds after delivery.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Attachment From First Contact Sender Opened From Mail Cache
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection_delivery:
#     direction: 'inbound'
#     attachment_extension|in:
#       - '.iso'
#       - '.img'
#       - '.lnk'
#       - '.htm'
#     sender_first_seen: 'true'
#   selection_open:
#     event_type: 'file_creation'
#     target_filename|contains:
#       - 'INetCache'
#       - 'Content.Outlook'
#   condition: selection_delivery and selection_open
# level: medium
falsePositives: Partners who send scanned invoices as disk image files because their scanner exports only that format.
Human resources teams who send password protected payroll documents to staff each month.
A colleague sending a shortcut or web page file for a legitimate internal tool.
Marketing platforms that attach a web page copy of a newsletter to the message.
tuningNotes: Profile which attachment types your organisation genuinely receives before you alert on them, and keep a per department exception list for finance and human resources. Add a filter for known partner mail servers with valid authentication results. Scope the alert to first contact senders and to messages that fail authentication. If you narrow the rule to the most dangerous extensions only, you lose the early test messages that carry harmless files, so keep a low severity branch that reports new senders with any attachment for trend review.
